note: Words and phrases that mark a sentence as carrying critical content (allergy, identity, consent, fasting state, a worsening sign, a structured handover). If a classifier names a NON-critical act for such a sentence, the sentence is not credited as that act: speech can never earn credit for a critical item, and a sentence that touches one is not allowed to earn credit under another act by being mislabelled. The sentence is still recorded. Lower-case regular expressions; reviewed with the act taxonomy (content/assessment/taxonomy.json). Version 2 (17 October 2026, after the first synthetic test run found seven sentences about an allergy reaction, a consent question and a handover that the language model still credited under ordinary acts): the allergens of content/ai/lexicon.json are cues too (loaded by guard.py), and the handover and consent cues cover "that's the background", "my suggestion" and "all right to go ahead". These were added after the synthetic test split was scored, so the as-scored numbers in reports/ai/classifier-bench-synthetic.json are those of version 1 and the effect of version 2 is reported separately as post hoc. Found by the classifier benchmark: the language model credited critical sentences under non-critical acts (docs/research/classifier_benchmark/qwen_critical_cases.md). Version 3 (18 October 2026): cues for the evasive wordings of tests/classifier_synthetic_v2/adversarial_critical.json (the tuning set; its sentences are listed in docs/research/classifier_benchmark), added after the v2 test split was scored once; the companion hold-out adversarial_critical_holdout.json was written before this change and is the check on whether the new cues generalise. The cost of the cues (credit removed from sentences that are not critical) is reported next to the gain. Two allergy cues ('foods you shouldn't have', 'made you poorly') were added after the one critical sentence the v3 hold-out still credited under an ordinary act was seen, so the v3 figures with them are post hoc.
